name: FAIR Data
title: FAIR Data
answer: FAIR data refers to research data and digital objects that are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable by both people and machines. The principles apply to datasets, software, models, and other research outputs held in repositories. In the context of AI research, FAIR data supports reproducible training, evaluation, and comparison of models. The scope includes metadata, persistent identifiers, and clear licensing rather than open access alone. A dataset can be FAIR while still having access controls.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: FAIR data refers to research data and digital objects that are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable by both people and machines. The principles apply to datasets, software, models, and other research outputs held in repositories. In the context of AI research, FAIR data supports reproducible training, evaluation, and comparison of models. The scope includes metadata, persistent identifiers, and clear licensing rather than open access alone. A dataset can be FAIR while still having access controls.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: FAIR data typically runs on repository platforms that assign persistent identifiers such as DOIs and expose structured metadata through standard protocols. These systems rely on catalogues, search indexes, and APIs that allow machine queries without needing to know the data location in advance. Storage may be local, cloud based, or federated across institutional and disciplinary repositories. Authentication and authorisation layers handle access where data cannot be fully public. The infrastructure must support versioning and provenance records so that a given dataset can be cited and retrieved over time.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Making data FAIR is a curation task rather than a single technical step. Researchers and data stewards describe datasets with rich metadata, use controlled vocabularies and ontologies, and link data to related code, papers, and models. Interoperability is achieved by adopting community standards for formats and semantics, such as schema.org or domain specific ontologies. Reusability requires clear data usage licences, provenance information, and enough context about how the data was collected or generated. The work often happens at deposit time in a repository, with automated checks for missing fields or broken links.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in FAIR data centre on the difference between findable metadata and accessible content. A dataset can be indexed and described while the underlying files remain restricted, which protects privacy, commercial confidentiality, or Indigenous data sovereignty. Licences must be machine readable and explicit about reuse, and provenance records should show who created, modified, or aggregated the data. Repositories and institutions carry responsibility for long term preservation, access control, and handling of sensitive personal data under relevant regulations. Risk also includes data misuse, re identification, and the spread of incorrect or biased information if provenance is weak.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: FAIR data is moving toward greater machine actionability, where automated agents can discover, assess, and combine datasets with less human mediation. Research communities are aligning FAIR with the needs of AI training pipelines, including data cards, model cards, and standardised evaluation splits. Expect tighter links between data repositories and computational environments so that a dataset can be pulled directly into a reproducible workflow. The emphasis is shifting from static deposit to living data objects that update with new versions, corrections, and linked results. Long term, FAIR will likely become a baseline expectation for any dataset used in published AI research.
